holding: For the foregoing reasons, the instant Constitutional Petition alongwith the two connected petitions challenging the Impugned Notifications are dismissed. The Constitutional Petitions filed by the Petitioner Students, seeking implementation of the Impugned Notifications are allowed with a direction to the PM&DC and the Institutions concerned to implement the Impugned Notifications in accordance with their terms, to the extent applicable to the respective Petitioner Students. Any consequential claim for adjustment or refund shall be given effect to by the Petitioner Institutions/Colleges within a period of 30 working days from 42 Government of the Punjab through Chief Secretary, Lahore and others v. Ashtar Ausaf Ali & Barrister Muhammad Umar Riaz, ASCs assisted by M/s. Saqib Haroon Chishti, Barrister Asad Rahim Khan, Nimra Arshad, Mian Ali Tariq Rehman, Faiz-e-Azhar, Ch. Mukhtar Ahmad Gondal and Raja Asif Ali, Advocates Respondents by: For Respondent/PM&DC Barrister Haris Azmat, ASC assisted by Barrister Hasnain Ali Khan, Ali Khizer, Barrister Malika Akhtar, Barrister Muhammad Umer Arif, Syed Abdullah Bukhari & Barrister Maryam Omer, Advocates For PM&DC in W.P. Through this judgment, I intend to decide the following Constitutional Petitions filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan ("Constitution"): Constitutional Petitions filed by Petitioner Institutions i. W.P No.43022 of 2026 ii. W.P No.43017 of 2026 iii. W.P No.47614 of 2026 Constitutional Petitions filed by Petitioner Students 1 i. W.P No. 30724 of 2026 ii. W.P No. 34032 of 2026 iii. W.P No. 34705 of 2026 iv. W.P No. 41583 of 2026 v. W.P No. 48957 of 2026 vi. W.P No. 50321 of 2026 vii. W.P No. 50670 of 2026 viii. W.P No. 56218 of 2026 ix. W.P No. 58776 of 2026 x. W.P No. 58942 of 2026 xi. W.P No. 60178 of 2026 xii. W.P No. 61874 of 2026 1 Some of the Constitutional Petitions have been filed by the parents/guardians of the Students seeking to enforce the fundamental rights of the students. Page 3

The instant Constitutional Petition and two (02) connected petitions seek to challenge the notifications dated 28.04.2025, 06.10.2025 and 11.03.2026 (the “Impugned Notifications”) issued by the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council ("PM&DC"), whereby, the Council proceeded to enhance and approve the fee structure of the Private Medical and Dental Institutions. Twelve (12) other petitions have been filed by the students or their parents, seeking implementation of the Impugned Notifications. Since, all these Constitutional Petitions involve the common questions of law viz the authority and jurisdiction of PM&DC to regulate the Private Medical and Dental Institutions/Colleges for determining the tuition fee under the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Act, 2022 ("PM&DC Act") read with Rules & Regulations framed in terms of the provisions contained in Section 47 of the PM&DC Act i.e. the PM&DC Medical and Dental under Graduate Education (Admissions, Curriculum and Conduct) Policy and Regulations, 2025 (“the “Regulations, 2025”). For convenience, the petitioners challenging the Impugned Notifications shall be referred to as the "Petitioner Institutions" and the petitioners seeking implementation of the Impugned Notifications as the "Petitioner Students":
For the purpose of this judgment, the facts of the present case shall suffice.

Briefly, the controversy originates from the imposition of tuition-fee limits by the PM&DC for Private Medical and Dental Colleges. It is of note that vide Notification dated 28.04.2025, the PM&DC decided to cap/fix the tuition fee with ancillary matters for MBBS and BDS Programs offered by Private Medical and Dental Colleges at Rs.18,00,000/- for all sessions with a 5% increase for session 2025 and subsequent increases based on the Consumer Price Index (“CPI”) Inflation Rate from Session 2026 onwards, whereas, vide Notification dated 06.10.2025, the tuition fee for session 2025-26 was capped at Rs.18,90,000/-.

The Petitioner Students complained against the overcharging of the exorbitant fees and other unauthorized amounts by the University Medical and Dental College, Faisalabad i.e. the present Petitioner Institution, and approached the Regulator i.e. PM&DC in terms of paragraph 5 of the Page 4 Notification dated 11.03.2026, seeking enforcement of the upper-cap of the maximum fee. The PM&DC initiated proceedings under the PM&DC Act against the delinquent colleges, which prompted the filing of the Constitutional Petitions by the Petitioner Institutions. In the meanwhile, the Petitioner Students also filed Constitutional Petitions for availing an efficacious remedy due to the adverse actions taken against the Petitioner Students by the non-compliant colleges due to students’ reservations against demand of unauthorized and illegal exorbitant fees and other hidden charges thrust upon the Petitioner Students or their parents.

The Petitioner Institutions claim that their institutions had independently determined and publicly declared fee structures for their respective programs under Section 20(7) of the PM&DC Act. The Petitioner Institutions question the Council’s subsequent intervention in those fee structures, including the revised fee determination made vide Notification dated 11.03.2026, on the ground that no authority or jurisdiction vests with the Council to cap or fix tuition fee under the PM&DC Act, therefore, the provisions contained in the Regulations, 2025, sought to be relied upon to exercise such authority are inconsequential since, as contended by the Petitioner Institutions, any Rules or Regulations framed beyond the statutory sphere of the main enactment are without any lawful effect. The challenge extends to the application of the prescribed limits to students already enrolled under previously declared fee structures.

In the petitions filed by the Petitioner Students, the relief sought is implementation of the Impugned Notifications. Thus, the connected matters present opposing claims concerning a common regulatory measure: the Petitioner Institutions seek to displace it, while the Petitioner Students seek its enforcement. The validity of the Impugned Notifications requires determination before the consequential relief in the students’ petitions can be settled, subject to its applicability to the students concerned.

Learned counsels for the Petitioner Institutions contend that the Council is a creature of statute and can exercise only those powers which are specifically conferred upon it by the legislature; add that neither the general regulatory description in Section 6 of PM&DC Act nor the powers under Page 5 Sections 9, 20 and 47 of PM&DC Act and Regulation 9 of the Regulations, 2025, authorize fee fixation; argue that sub-section (7) of Section 20 of PM&DC Act explicitly recognizes the colleges’ exclusive authority to determine and declare fees, whereas, sub-section (8) thereof merely requires submission of financial statements, the proposed fee structure and its justification, without expressly authorizing approval, substitution or prescription of a uniform ceiling. Learned counsels seek to rely upon the principle that a specific provision prevails over a general one and that an omission in the former cannot be supplied through the latter. On the requirement that every exercise of public power must have a traceable legal source, reliance is placed upon the recent judgments passed by the Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan in the cases of Bayazid Khan2 and Muhammad Abdul Qadoos3; contend that a uniform ceiling disregards differences in infrastructure, teaching hospitals, faculty costs and institutional requirements. Learned counsels submit that any Rules or Regulations framed beyond the statutory sphere of the main enactment are without any lawful effect. Reliance in this regard has been placed upon the cases of Pakistan Broadcasters Association4 & Haji Ghulam Zamin.5

Learned counsel for the Petitioner Institutions argue that Article 18 of the Constitution requires a restriction to pursue a compelling interest, which compelling interest must be narrowly tailored for the purpose of ensuring the Constitutional safeguards supplied therein. They submit that cheaper medical education, without establishing the necessary connection to a compelling governmental interest, is insufficient; that scholarships and public-sector institutions are available alternatives and that a fee ceiling may impair the very standards which are required to be maintained by virtue of the provisions contained in the PM&DC Act and accreditation rules framed thereunder. Reliance in this regard is placed upon a recent judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan in Shabbir Hussain’s6 case, 2 The Chief Secretary, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and others v. Bayazid Khan Kharooti, [C.P.L.A. No.217-Q of 2023, decided on 05.03.2026. 3 Muhammad Abdul Qadoos v. Province of Punjab and others (F.C.P.L.A. No. 507 of 2025) 4 PEMRA v. Pakistan Broadcasters Association (PLD 2023 SC 378) 5 Haji Ghulam Zamin v. A.B.Khondkar (PLD 1965 Dhaka 156) 6 Peshawar High Court Bar Association through its Secretary General, Peshawar v. Shabbir Hussain and another, [F.C.P.L.A. Nos.379, 380, 384 and 389 of 2025, decided on 31.03.2026]. Page 6 Muhammad Imran’s7 case and a judgment from American jurisdiction in the Citizens United8 case.

Learned counsels further submit that the impugned measures operate retrospectively and disturb fee structures declared for the entire program of study by the Institutions, while exercising authority under sub-section (7) of Section 20 of PM&DC Act. Reliance in this respect is placed upon the cases of Trustees’ of Port of Karachi9 and Imtiaz Ahmad10. Learned counsels contend that Private Medical & Dental Colleges have been singled out in comparison with Private Institutions offering engineering and business programs, contrary to Article 25 of the Constitution; add that the PM&DC Act is a regulatory enactment rather than beneficial legislation and its burdens cannot be enlarged through a liberal construction. In rebuttal to the plea of acquiescence, agitated through the reply filed by PM&DC, learned counsels for the Petitioner Institutions attempted to argue that neither the consent nor the participation of the Pakistan Association of Private Medical and Dental Institutions (“PAMI”) can confer statutory jurisdiction upon the Council, which jurisdiction does not vest otherwise. Learned counsels have overwhelmingly argued that the revised regulatory fee is an erosion of the rights of Private Medical and Dental Institutions to determine the fee for running and managing their Institutions. Thus, while assuming that no jurisdiction or authority vests with the Council under the PM&DC Act for determination of the fee structure of the Private Medical and Dental Institutions, since no such authority arises out of the statutory provisions, therefore, the same can neither be supplied by relying upon the principle of ‘Casus Omissus’ nor by ‘reading in’ any such authority in the provisions contained in the Statute. Reliance is placed upon the cases of Gul Tez Khan Marwat11 and Aam Log Itehad12.

While seeking to draw attention to the Indian jurisprudence developed over the years viz the concept of fundamental need of education and the 7 Mohammad Imran v. Province of Sindh (2019 SCMR 1753) 8 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (558 U.S. 310 (2010)). 9 Trustees’ of Port of Karachi v. Zaffar Zaid Ahmad (1988 SCMR 810). 10 Imtiaz Ahmad v. PPSC (PLD 2006 SC 472). 11 Gul Tez Khan Marwat v. Registrar Peshawar High Court (PLD 2021 SC 391) 12 Aam Log Itehad v. Election Commission of Pakistan (PLD 2022 SC 39) Page 7 elements of freedom of trade, as encapsulated in Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India and the elements of prohibition of profiteering, perhaps by preempting the converse reliance by the other side, learned counsels for the Petitioner Institutions have extensively referred to the cases of Mohini Jain,13 Unni Krishnan,14 T.M.A. Pai Foundation,15 Islamic Academy of Education16 and P.A. Inamdar17, and contend that institutional autonomy includes formulation of a reasonable fee structure, subject to prevention of capitation fee and profiteering. They sought to distinguish the case of Modern Dental College18 on the ground that the respective legislation in India, which was the subject matter legislation under consideration, expressly empowered a separate committee to determine fees and provided institutional safeguards. Learned counsels have also referred to the United Kingdom’s separation of medical standard-setting from the statutory arrangements governing fee limits and to the distinct fee-regulatory enactments of Indian States, to emphasise the necessity of statutory authority.19

Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent-PM&DC opposes the petitions of Petitioner Institutions and submits that fee regulation involves financial scrutiny, accreditation standards, student protection and consistency across recognized medical and dental institutions, thus, the matters squarely fall within the regulatory and statutory responsibility of the PM&DC and its Council acted lawfully while issuing the Impugned Notifications as well as the Regulations, 2025; contends that while judicial review remains available against demonstrated illegality, the Courts have always followed the principle of restraint in exercise of such jurisdiction where the policy matters are involved. In support, he places reliance upon Hafsa Habib Qureshi v. Amir Hamza (PLD 2024 SC 780), Sundas and others v. Khyber Medical University and others (2024 SCMR 46), Aina v. 13 Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) 3 SCC 666. 14 Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) 1 SCC 645. 15 T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) 8 SCC 481. 16 Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697. 17 P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) 6 SCC 537. 18 Modern Dental College and Research Centres v. State of Madhya Pardesh and others (2016) 7 SCC 353 19 Medical Act 1983 (United Kingdom), Sections 1, 4–7; Higher Education and Research Act 2017 (United Kingdom), Section 10 and Schedule. Note: The comparative enactments are referred to as part of the petitioners’ submissions; their institutional arrangements do not govern construction of the PM&DC Act. Page 8 Principal, Peshawar Medical College High School (2025 SCMR 108), Khyber Medical University v. Aimal Khan (PLD 2022 SC 92) and University of Health Sciences, Lahore v. Arsalan Ali (2016 SCMR 134). Learned counsel has also raised the objection of laches, while submitting that the notifications dated 28.04.2025, 06.10.2025 and 11.03.2026 were challenged only after issuance of the enforcement notice dated 04.08.2026, without satisfactorily explaining the intervening delay.

The respondent-PM&DC maintains that the fee determinations were undertaken in exercise of its statutory regulatory functions. It further relies upon the participation of the PAMI, of which the petitioner medical college is stated to be a member, in meetings before the Special Committee constituted for the purpose, pursuant to earlier proceedings before the Islamabad High Court. According to the respondent, those proceedings resulted in retrospective enhancement of the prescribed fee and were not disclosed in the petition. The Petitioner Institutions dispute the asserted benefit; their rebuttal explains that the notification dated 11.03.2026 revised an earlier regulatory determination but did not enhance the higher fees which the colleges had independently declared. These competing positions provide the background to the legal controversy; the existence of jurisdiction must nevertheless be determined from the PM&DC Act.

Learned counsel for the PM&DC further submits that the authority and jurisdiction of the Council to review, regulate and enforce tuition-fee structures emanate from a harmonious reading of Sections 9, 20 and 47 of the PM&DC Act; argues that the residual powers preserved under sub- section (1) of Section 9 of the PM&DC Act, the express preservation of generality in sub-section (2) of Section 9, the fee-related obligations under sub-sections (7) & (8) of Section 20 and the regulation-framing power under Section 47(2)(g) of the PM&DC Act constitute a complete regulatory framework; contends that Section 20(7) cannot be read as an unregulated and unbridled authorization for colleges to conclusively determine fees; rather, it must be read with Section 20(8), which requires submission of financial statements, the proposed fee structure and its justification to the Council; further contends that the statutory sequence contemplates a Page 9 proposal by the college, its justification before the Council and public declaration of the fee subject to regulatory oversight and nowhere does the PM&DC Act declare the determination made by the Colleges to be final or immune from scrutiny by the Council; further adds that Regulation 9 of the Regulations, 2025 expressly requires colleges to charge tuition fee duly approved by PM&DC, which may determine, review and regulate such fee to ensure transparency and prevent exploitation; maintains that the regulation operationalizes powers already conferred by the parent statute and does not create an independent jurisdiction. On the scope of regulatory and delegated powers, reliance is placed upon Naresh Chandra Agrawal v. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and others ((2024) 13 SCC 241), Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited v. Telecom Regulatory Authority of India and others ((2014) 3 SCC 222), Deepak Theatre, Dhuri v. State of Punjab and others (1992 Supp (1) SCC 684), Jameel Sweets v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2020 PTD 752) and Pakistan Medical and Dental Council and others v. Muhammad Fahad Malik and 3 others (2018 SCMR 1956).

Explaining the chronology, which led to the issuance of the Impugned Notifications, learned counsel submits that a Committee on Medical Education was constituted through the Prime Minister’s Office U.O. dated 20.05.2024 under the chairmanship of the Deputy Prime Minister. On 27.03.2025, a sub-committee was constituted to examine private medical colleges’ fee structures and audited financial statements; submits that the ensuing deliberations resulted in the notification dated 28.04.2025, prescribing a tuition-fee ceiling of Rs.18,00,000/- for all sessions and linking subsequent enhancement with the CPI. Thereafter, the notification dated 06.10.2025 permitted a 5% increase of fee for the session 2025 with subsequent annual enhancement from the session 2026 onwards linked with the CPI; adds that in the follow-up meeting held on 18.12.2025, the ceiling was reaffirmed as inclusive of all ancillary charges, while institutions were permitted to seek conditional enhancement upto Rs.25,00,000/- upon justification supported by audited accounts. According to learned counsel for PM&DC, the petitioner colleges, alongwith other institutions, applied for Page 10 enhancement of the fee by submitting the supporting documents in the form of Audited Financial Statements, thus, the case of the Petitioner Institution(s) was considered by the Committee specifically constituted for the said purpose, comprising representatives of PAMI. The matter was considered by the Fee Justification Committee on 18.02.2026 and following scrutiny of the financial statements and the Committee’s recommendations, the Notification dated 11.03.2026 prescribed the applicable fee ceilings, fixing the petitioner college’s annual tuition fee at Rs.20,26,341/- for University Medical and Dental College, Faisalabad and Rs.20,52,099/- for FMH College of Medicine and Dentistry, Lahore (Petitioner Institutions); adds that the enforcement notice dated 04.08.2026 was issued when the fee displayed on the petitioner college’s official website was found to exceed the approved ceiling. Learned counsel further submits that the Petitioner Institutions are members of PAMI, which, pursuant to earlier proceedings before the Islamabad High Court, participated in meetings before the Special Committee/Council and secured retrospective enhancement of the prescribed fee; contends that these material facts were concealed while invoking the Constitutional jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution; thus, it is pleaded by learned counsel for PM&DC that the instant Constitutional Petitions filed by the Petitioner Institutions are liable to be dismissed on the sole ground of maintainability as the Petitioners’ hands are sullied with gross concealment, acquiescence and waiver; contends that, having appeared before the Council, submitted financial material and sought enhancement of fee through their representative association, the Petitioner Institutions acknowledged the regulatory authority of the Council and cannot now seek discretionary relief while withholding their participation in that process.

Learned counsel urges a construction advancing the protective object of the enactment i.e. PM&DC Act while placing reliance upon the judgments reported as Province of Sindh and others v. Azhar Ali and others (2026 PLC (C.S.) 1221), Employees Old-Age Benefits Institution, Lahore and others v. Muhammad Rafique and others (2026 PLC (Labour) 107), Jamila Dixit v. Sunil Sharan Dixit and others ((2025) 2 SCC 787), X v. Page 11 Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Government of NCT of Delhi and another ((2023) 9 SCC 433) and Union of India v. Prabhakaran Vijaya Kumar and others ((2008) 9 SCC 527). On the interpretation of corresponding statutory provisions, learned counsel places particular reliance upon Abwa Knowledge (Pvt.) Ltd. and another v. Federation of Pakistan and another (PLD 2021 Lahore 436) and the Division Bench judgment in Abwa Knowledge Village (Pvt.) Ltd. through Director and another v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, National Health Services and another (2021 MLD 1455), submitting that the requirement to justify a proposed fee structure carries the authority to review that structure if found unjustifiable. He also refers to Mohammad Imran and others v. Province of Sindh and others (2019 SCMR 1753) concerning school-fee regulation and Modern Dental College and Research Centre and others v. State of Madhya Pradesh and others ((2016) 7 SCC 353) in support of fee regulation and prevention of commercialization. He contends that permitting private colleges to charge fees entirely at their own discretion, unchecked by regulatory limits, would defeat the legislative object of the PM&DC Act; lastly submits that where two interpretations are possible, the construction sustaining the law ought to be preferred; relies upon Sher Muhammad Mughari and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2026 FCC 365), Federation of Pakistan and others v. Saleem Raza (PLD 2020 SC 320) and Sui Southern Gas Company Ltd. and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2018 SCMR 802). On the scope of delegated legislation and the legislative field, learned counsel has additionally referred to Muhammad Ali Ghori and another v. Government of Punjab and others (PLD 2023 Lahore 572), Uzair Ahmed v. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Public Service Commission and others (2026 PLC (C.S.) 371), Commissioner Inland Revenue, Lahore v. Coca Cola Pakistan Limited, Lahore (2022 PTD 1400) and Raja Amer Khan and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2025 SC 869). He finally prays for dismissal of the Constitutional Petition challenging the Impugned Notifications.
I have heard the learned counsels for the parties at considerable length and have perused the record with their able assistance. Page 12

The questions, which arise for determination by this Court are summed up as follows: i. Whether any mandate, statutory authority and jurisdiction vests with the PM&DC to cap/fix the tuition fee with ancillary matters for MBBS and BDS Programs offered by the Private Medical and Dental Institutions under the provisions contained in the PM&DC Act? ii. If so, whether such authority can cater for a generally applicable fee ceiling? iii. What is the effect of the objections founded upon Articles 18 & 25 of the Constitution and the temporal application of the measures? iv. What is the effect of participation of PAMI in the process of determination of fee structure by PM&DC and consequent withdrawal of the Constitutional Petitions filed before the Islamabad High Court, coupled with the alleged acquiescence and waiver and consequentially, the relief sought in the Constitutional Petition filed by Petitioner Students?

As evident, the grundnorm question, which needs to be answered at the outset is rooted in the objections raised by the Petitioner Institutions viz the authority and jurisdiction of the Council, therefore, the answer must come from the PM&DC Act, thus, the same is perused. The Preamble of the PM&DC Act declares its overarching objective to be the establishment of a uniform minimum standard of basic and higher qualifications in medicine and dentistry. This legislative objective finds its substantive manifestation in Section 20 of PM&DC Act, devoted to prescribing and maintaining educational standards. The Preamble and Section 20 read with Section 9 of the PM&DC Act are, therefore, united by a common legislative thread. Section 6 thereof expressly identifies the Council as the regulatory body for medical and dental profession, education and institutions. It is in this statutory setting that the significance of tuition fee and the legislative intention underlying Section 20 must be appreciated. In this respect, the true Page 13 appreciation of legislative scheme of PM&DC Act is particularly revealing as the mechanism concerning the tuition fee has been incorporated within Section 20 itself. Although its heading refers to ‘Standards of medical and dental education’, its substantive contents expressly address the elements of justification of proposed fee structure by the Council. Before dilating further on the subject, it is imperative to note that much emphasis was laid by the learned counsels for the Petitioner Institutions viz the limited scope of the provisions contained in Section 20 of the PM&DC Act as it was enthusiastically argued that the provision in question only deals with the authority and jurisdiction of accreditation of standards of medical and dental education. With respect, the contentions so raised are misconceived as the learned counsels have perhaps been carried away with a mere heading of the provision in question and skipped to appreciate its true import and contours. A heading of a provision may assist construction but cannot curtail the operative language. One must, therefore, read the provision in its true perspective, by its contents and objectives, rather than adopt a narrow or pedantic approach which excludes a subject expressly included by the Legislature; it is but a shorthand reference to the general subject matter involved; the headings and titles are not meant to take the place of the detailed provisions of the text, nor are they necessarily designed to be a reference guide or a synopsis. For interpretative purposes, they are of use only, when they shed light on some ambiguous word or phrase; they are but tools available for the resolution of a doubt and cannot undo or limit that which the text makes plain.20 If the language of a section is clear, headings are not to be taken into consideration.21 The view is now settled that the headings or titles prefixed to sections or groups of sections can be referred to in construing an Act of the legislature.22 The combined position emerging from the commentaries of the celebrated authors and jurists is that statutory headings are legitimate interpretative aids but are subordinate to the 20 see pp. 221–224 | Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts | 2012 Edition (Title-and-Headings Canon) | Antonin Scalia and Bryan A. Garner | Published by Thomson/West 21 see p. 55 | Interpretation of Statutes | Seventh Edition | N.S. Bindra 22 see pp. 152 and 155 | Principles of Statutory Interpretation | Ninth Edition (2004) | Justice G.P. Singh | Published by LexisNexis Page 14 operative text of the statute and cannot be invoked to curtail a power otherwise clearly conferred by the substantive provisions.

Having considered the arguments premised on the ‘Heading’ of Section 20 of PM&DC Act, the provisions contained in sub-sections (7) and (8) of Section 20 are of inescapable import and effect. A purposive analysis would manifest that both these provisions contemplate distinct but connected obligations. Public declaration of fixed tuition and ancillary fees protects the intending student by disclosing the financial commitment before admissions, whereas, the submission of financial statements by the Private Medical and Dental Institutions to the PM&DC, the proposed fee structure and its justification, subjects the financial basis of that proposal to regulatory consideration. The responsibility to declare the fee does not, by itself, confer immunity from scrutiny by the Council nor can the requirement of justification be reduced to mere notification of a decision, which the Council is bound to accept. The expressions “proposed fee structure” and “justification”, occurring in close syntactical proximity, are significant and not without the predominant purpose. The ordinary and lexical meaning of “proposed” is something put forward for consideration or adoption, whereas, the term “justification” denotes the adequate or sufficient reasons advanced in its support. The PM&DC Act does not separately define the words ‘proposed’ or ‘justification’, therefore, their meaning may be examined from their ordinary and lexical connotation and the judicial pronouncements in which these expressions have been considered, particularly in the context of fees charged by professional educational institutions. In the dictionary “A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles, edited by Sir James A.H. Murray, Volume VII (O, P), at p.1481”, the adjectival meaning of “proposed” is mentioned as “Put forward for consideration or adoption; intended, etc.”; it also explains ‘propose’, in the relevant sense, as putting forward a scheme or plan for consideration or adoption. Similarly, P. Ramanatha Aiyar, The Major Law Lexicon, 4th Edition, Volume 5 (P–R), at p.5459, explains “propose” as: ‘to offer, as a plan or scheme; to put or hold before one's mind, as a design or determination; to form, as a purpose.”. The judicial meaning collected in Words and Phrases, Permanent Edition, Page 15 Volume 34B, p.241, with reference to Hand v. Shaw, 50 N.Y.S. 117, similarly states that “propose” means to offer as a plan or scheme and specifically records that it: “necessarily does not mean an accomplished fact.” Likewise, Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases, Sixth Edition, Volume 2, while referring to Mainwaring v. Trustees of Henry Smith’s Charity ([1996] 2 All ER 220) records that the expression “proposes” denotes: “a state of mind between mere consideration of a possible course of action and a fixed and irrevocable determination to pursue that course of action.” Thus, the ordinary, lexical and judicial meanings place a proposal beyond mere contemplation, but distinguish it from an accomplished or irrevocably concluded determination. The statutory setting, which proceeds to complete the intent and purpose of the proposal to be submitted with audited financial accounts to the Council, is encapsulated in the words ‘justification to the Council’ as occurring immediately after the proposed fee structure to be submitted by the colleges. The relevant lexical meaning of “justification” centers upon the showing of a sufficient or adequate reason for the thing proposed or done. Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases, Sixth Edition, Volume 2, p.1379, defines “justification” as: “an affirming or showing good reason in Court why he did such a thing as he is called to answer.” Likewise, P. Ramanatha Aiyar's Advanced Law Lexicon, 4th Edition, Volume 3 (J–P), p.2624, explains “Justification” as: “A maintaining or showing of good reason in Court why one did such a thing for which he is called to answer.” The same entry explains “Justified” as: “Done on adequate reasons, sufficiently supported by credible evidence, when weighed by unprejudiced mind, guided by common sense and by correct rules of law.” The latter meaning was considered by the Supreme Court of India in Raj Kapoor v. Laxman, [AIR 1980 SC 605 = (1980) 2 SCC 175], wherein the Court referred to the meaning of “justified” as being done on adequate reasons sufficiently supported by credible evidence and further observed: “Lexically, the sense is clear. An act is justified by law if it is warranted, validated and made blameless by law.” The said Court also reproduced the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary meaning of “justification” as: “The showing in court that one had sufficient reason for doing that which he is called to answer; the Page 16 ground for such a plea.” The relevant lexical and judicial sense of “justification”, therefore, is the ‘showing of adequate or sufficient reason in support of the matter in question’. Thus, the proposed fee structure laid before the Council, which is accompanied by financial statements and addressed to the Council, supplies both the material and the reasons for an evaluative exercise to be undertaken by the Council and submission of such proposal and material by the Private Medical and Dental Institutions, is not meant for passive record-keeping. If the Council could neither question an inadequate justification nor require correction of the resulting fee, the statutory exercise would be deprived of effective consequence. The construction, which gives operation to each expression is to recognize scrutiny followed, where warranted, by approval, modification or rejection of the proposal. The well settled rule of interpretation against the absence of any surplusage in a statute and harmonious construction supports that reading.23

Having considered the true import of the provisions contained in sub- sections (7) and (8) of Section 20, read with preamble of the PM&DC Act, the reliance is also placed upon the unfettered, all-encompassing authority of the Council ensuing from the provisions contained in sub-sections (1) & (2) of Section 9 of PM&DC Act. The governing part of sub-section (1) of Section 9 mandates that ‘the Council shall have all powers not expressly vested in any other authority or officer by any other law where such powers not expressly mentioned in this Act are necessary for the performance of its functions”. Likewise, sub-section (2) of Section 9 states that “without prejudice to the generality of powers of the Council and notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force”, the Council’s powers have been further enumerated under the sub-section (2). In order to obviate the possibility of any misconceived inference, it is of note that the Council does not only exercise the functions for achieving the objects and purposes of PM&DC Act but it also has the powers of general supervision. The distinction between ‘generality’ and ‘enumeration’ is answered by the statutory language. Section 9(1) preserves powers necessary 23 Antonin Scalia and Bryan A. Garner, Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts (Thomson/West, 2012), pp.174 and 180, Surplusage Canon and Harmonious-Reading Canon. Page 17 for performance of the Council’s functions, subject to the qualification respecting powers expressly vested elsewhere by law. Section 9(2) enumerates particular functions “Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing powers”. To treat that enumeration as exhaustive would reverse the express legislative direction, which cannot be given any countenance by any stretch of interpretation. The enumerated powers supplement the general authority. The well settled principle of ‘generality v. enumeration’ postulates that where a statute confers a general power to make rules or regulations, the subsequent enumeration of specific matters, particularly when preceded by the expression “without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power” [as also occurring in sub-section (2) of Section 9] is merely illustrative and not exhaustive. Such enumeration neither restricts nor curtails the ambit of the general power, which may legitimately extend to matters not expressly enumerated, provided they fall within the purposes and scheme of the parent statute. However, the exercise of such power must remain ancillary to the statute and cannot enlarge its scope or create substantive rights, obligations or disabilities not contemplated by the legislature.24 The authority and jurisdiction of Council flow from the function expressly contemplated in Section 20(8) read with Section 9 (1) & (2) of the PM&DC Act; it is not created solely by invoking public interest, which aspect of the matter cannot be ignored either as the medical education is not a luxury and instead it is one of the essentials for any nation to survive nor can the medical profession be rendered as a money-making tool as the medical professionals deal with the noble cause of dealing with the human life and health. The legal source required by Bayazid Khan and Muhammad Abdul Qadoos supra is thus identified in the PM&DC Act itself.

Thus, a conjoint reading of the Preamble, Sections 6 and 9 and sub- sections (7) and (8) of Section 20 establishes that the PM&DC possesses the authority and jurisdiction to scrutinize, regulate and determine tuition fee, 24 Emperor v. Government of the Philippine Islands (277 U.S. 189, 206–207 (1928)); Afzal Ullah v. State of Uttar Pradesh (AIR 1964 SC 264); Rohtak and Hissar Districts Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh (AIR 1966 SC 1471); K. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu ((1985) 2 SCC 116); D.K. Trivedi and Sons v. State of Gujarat (1986 Supp SCC 20); Academy of Nutrition Improvement v. Union of India ((2011) 8 SCC 274); Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. v. Telecom Regulatory Authority of India ((2014) 3 SCC 222); Naresh Chandra Agrawal v. Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (2024 INSC 94, paras 27–37). Page 18 including imposition of permissible limits within that statutory framework. The “proposed fee” and its “justification” have regulatory consequences; the contrary construction would leave the Council with a duty to receive the proposal but without the authority necessary to evaluate it effectively. The Petitioner Institutions’ challenge founded upon absence of statutory competence is, therefore, repelled.

Thus, the Petitioner Institutions’ reliance upon generalia specialibus non derogant [General provisions do not derogate from special provisions] does not lead to a different result. That principle resolves a conflict between general and specific provisions. No such conflict is established merely because the specific provision requires a proposal and its justification without separately enumerating every consequential step. Equally, expressio unius est exclusio alterius [The express mention of one thing implies the exclusion of another] cannot defeat the express preservation of generality in Section 9(2) of PM&DC Act. Sections 9 and 20 of PM&DC Act must operate harmoniously as neither may be read so as to extinguish the function assigned by the other. A ceiling is not outside the Council’s competence merely because it applies generally. Its formulation must, nevertheless, retain a rational connection with the relevant financial considerations and must not defeat the statutory opportunity to justify a proposed structure. Common regulation and institutional financial justification must operate together.

The reference may also be made to a judgment of a learned Division Bench of this Court reported as Abwa Knowledge Village25, whereby, while interpreting the pari materia provisions of Sections 19(7) & (8) of the Pakistan Medical Commission Act, 2020, the authority of the regulator i.e. Pakistan Medical Commission, was discussed and approved vis-à-vis the determination of the fee structure after reviewing and determining the justification of the fee proposed by the Private Medical and Dental Institutions. The relevant reasoning of the Division Bench connects fee scrutiny with the prevention of exploitation and the relationship between the 25 Abwa Knowledge Village (Pvt.) Ltd. through Director and another v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, National Health Services and another (2021 MLD 1455); Page 19 fee and institutional facilities. The retention of the material expressions in the PM&DC Act makes that reasoning pertinent, without treating the earlier enactment and its subordinate instruments as presently governing the controversy.

In addition to and without prejudice to the foregoing, it is appropriate to consider as to what a statutory power to ‘regulate’ an activity includes, particularly in view of the scope and contours of the authority and jurisdiction of a Regulator when the subject matter regulated activity relates to the issues directly associated with public good? Whether it extends to prescribing standards, to prohibition and to enforcement measures such as inspection, standardization, accreditation, recognition and/or de-recognition but does not include anything else, which is not expressly explicated or enumerated by the statute. The word ‘regulate’ has no fixed meaning and Courts read it according to the object and context of the statute.26 On the substantive reach of a power to regulate a trade, commodity or activity, the dominant view is wide: in the absence of restrictive words, the power is plenary over the subject and may, in some circumstances, extend to prohibition.27 A narrower line treats regulation as the making of general rules in advance and holds that it does not, without more, include adjudication of individual disputes,28 or the prohibition of a lawful activity for an object unconnected with how it is carried on.29 The two lines are reconcilable. The narrow cases concern who may decide individual disputes under a power to regulate; the wide cases concern the content of the general rules that may be made. Enforcement powers incidental to a regulatory scheme may be implied where the statute’s general enabling words allow, but implication is confined to what is necessary. The power to regulate 26 K. National Industrial Relations Commission (PLD 1982 SC 125). 27 Slattery v. Naylor (1888) 13 App Cas 446 (PC) , Sri Venkata Seetaramanjaneya Rice and Oil Mills and others v. State of Andhra Pradesh (AIR 1964 SC 1781 = (1964) 7 SCR 456), K. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu and another (AIR 1985 SC 660), Mahmood Majid, Director, Asia Flour Mills (Pvt.) Ltd., Bahawalpur v. The State and 3 others (PLD 1998 Lahore 296). 28 Karachi Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. v. National Industrial Relations Commission (PLD 1982 SC 125), Pakistan Burmah Shell Ltd. v. Syed Akhlaque Hussain and another (PLD 1965 SC 527) Page 20 carries with it full power over the things subject to regulation and in absence of restrictive words, the power must be regarded as plenary over the entire subject. The power to regulate implies the power to check and may imply the power to prohibit under certain circumstances as where the best or only efficacious regulation consists of suppression. To ‘regulate’ has different shades of meaning and must take its colour from the context in which it is used having regard to the purpose and object of the legislation and the Court must necessarily keep in view the mischief which the legislature seeks to remedy. The present question concerns financial conditions upon which regulated education is imparted, a subject expressly addressed in Section 20, read with Section 9(1) of the PM&DC Act and the Regulations, 2025 framed under Section 47 of the PM&DC Act; it does not involve assumption of an unrelated jurisdiction to decide private disputes.

The submissions concerning delegated legislation and beneficial construction must be kept within their proper limits. Neither a presumption in favour of validity nor a liberal construction authorizes a subordinate instrument to enlarge the parent enactment. Conversely, the PM&DC Act’s regulatory character does not require its student-protective provisions to be deprived of operation. Its disclosure requirements, prohibition of additional payments and restrictions upon enhancement have protective consequences. It is unnecessary to classify the whole enactment as exclusively beneficial or exclusively burdensome. However, while construing a statute or a provision therein, having a beneficial object, that object must be kept in view so that the protection intended by the legislature is not defeated by a narrow or strict literal interpretation. It is trite that there is nothing which could prevent the Courts in Pakistan from adopting beneficial construction as against literal whenever a controversy arises in this respect.30 Where two constructions are reasonably open, preference is to be given to the one which advances the remedy and gives effect to the beneficial purpose of the enactment, consistent with its language and scheme.31 The Supreme Court of Pakistan has accordingly construed the beneficial legislation liberally in favour of its intended beneficiaries, while recognizing that beneficial construction does 30 Haji Kadir Bux and others v. Province of Sind and another (1982 SCMR 582). 31 Province of Punjab v. Qaisar Iqbal and others (PLD 2018 Lahore 198)[Full Bench], Page 21 not dispense with express statutory conditions.32 Needless to observe that it is also well settled that such an interpretative approach cannot validate delegated legislation, which travels beyond the powers conferred by the parent enactment; the protective object must be effectuated within and not outside, the statutory framework.33 In the instant case, as adumbrated above, neither the Impugned Notifications issued by the PM&DC nor the Regulations, 2025 can be termed as beyond the sphere and scope of the PM&DC Act, therefore, the object sought to be achieved by maintaining a balance between the financial exigencies, operations of the medical and dental institutions and the protection of the students from charging of exorbitant fees and charges by placing a check on the profiteering, cannot be condemned and set aside.

Adverting to the grounds raised by the Petitioner Institutions on the premise of Article 18 of the Constitution, the same must be considered against the standards identified in Peshawar High Court Bar Association’s34 case, as relied upon by the Petitioner Institutions. There is no cavil with the settled position of law that a restriction upon economic activity must pursue a compelling interest and be narrowly tailored. The possession of regulatory power does not, by itself, answer that enquiry. The relevant interest here is the integrity and continuity of regulated medical education, including protection against unjustified financial demands, while ensuring the resources necessary to maintain educational standards. It is not confined to increasing the number of doctors. Scholarships and public-sector expansion may serve educational access but do not perform the statutory function of testing the justification of fees demanded by regulated institutions. At the same time, the Council must account for legitimate institutional costs; a measure which disables compliance with its own educational standards cannot be justified by affordability alone. 32 Amir Sultan and others v. Adjudicating Authority-III, EOBI, Islamabad and others (2024 SCMR 826), Don Basco High School v. Assistant Director, EOBI (PLD 1989 SC 128); Lahore Race Club v. Deputy Director, EOBI (1998 SCMR 1571). 33 Shaukat Mahmood v. Election Commission of Pakistan (PLD 2024 SC 653); Waseem Riaz and 119 others v. Ministry of Capital Administration and Development (2019 PLC (C.S.) 403). 34 Peshawar High Court Bar Association through its Secretary General, Peshawar v. Shabbir Hussain and another, F.C.P.L.A. Nos.379, 380, 384 and 389 of 2025, decided on 31.03.2026 (Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan), Page 22

The scope and contours of Article 18 of the Constitution have authoritatively been examined and enunciated by the Supreme Court in Pakcom Limited,35 Arshad Mehmood36 and Dossani Travels,37 wherein it has consistently been held that the freedom to carry on a lawful profession, trade or business, though constitutionally guaranteed, is neither absolute nor unfettered. The power of the State or that of a Regulator to regulate such activity is nevertheless circumscribed by the requirement that the restrictions imposed must be reasonable, non-arbitrary and bear a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. The Constitutional scheme thus contemplates a balance between the rights of an individual undertaking an economic activity and the larger interests of society. More pertinently, in Mohammad Imran’s38 case, the Supreme Court of Pakistan, while considering the Constitutional validity of statutory provisions regulating tuition fees charged by private educational institutions, recognized that such institutions, notwithstanding their commercial character, remain amenable to regulation under Article 18 of the Constitution, including regulation and control of fees and matters incidental thereto. It was held that the power to regulate must be exercised fairly and reasonably and its exercise remains open to judicial scrutiny where the restriction is shown to be arbitrary, excessive or beyond the legitimate limits of regulation. The principle is equally applicable to Private Medical and Dental Institutions, whose entitlement to propose tuition fees cannot be divorced from the statutory framework governing medical education. The Constitutional protection afforded by Article 18 of the Constitution does not, therefore, immunize the Petitioner Institutions against fee regulation undertaken in furtherance of a legitimate public interest. The recognition of the State's authority to impose reasonable conditions upon regulated economic activity also finds support in Abbas Haider Naqvi’s39 case, wherein, the Supreme Court of Pakistan acknowledged the Legislature's competence to regulate trades and businesses in the public 35 Pakcom Limited and others v. Having ventured to present themselves for seeking enhancement of the tuition fee and after securing the retrospective enhancement for the previous session/years, the Petitioner Institutions cannot now be allowed to turn volta-face and invoke the extraordinary equitable jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution.

The Petitioner Institutions have also ventured to rely upon the principles of proportionality in their favour. The inquiry, however, is not concluded merely by identifying an interference with economic freedom. It requires consideration whether the measure pursues a compelling public interest, is rationally connected to that interest, goes no further than reasonably necessary to achieve it and maintains a fair balance between the burden imposed upon the institutions and the public benefit sought. These aspects are interrelated and must be assessed in the context of the right asserted, the statutory objective, the regulatory setting and the material placed before the Court.40 In the instant case, the relevant public interest is the protection of students against unjustified financial demands together with 40 see pp.278–279 | Proportionality: A Guiding Principle in Public Health Law, Ethics, and Policy | (2026) | Edited by Nikola Biller-Andorno, Julian W. März, Corine Mouton-Dorey & Stéphanie Dagron | Published by Oxford University Press. Page 26 the maintenance of the standards and continuity of medical education. The process preceding the Notification dated 11.03.2026 involved scrutiny of the audited accounts submitted by the Petitioner Institutions by a specially constituted Fee Justification Committee followed by its consideration and decision thereon by the Council. The resulting framework distinguished institutions according to the material they submitted and their eligibility for enhancement. Moreover, the joint statement placed before the Islamabad High Court contemplated conditional enhancement, upon audited accounts, up to PKR 2.5 million and provided for CPI-linked adjustments. The measure, therefore, was accompanied by means to consider institutional circumstances; it was not an unqualified prohibition upon recovery of fees sufficient to meet justified costs. The balancing inquiry must also take account of the record concerning the Petitioner Institutions themselves. Positive profits do not, by themselves, determine whether every fee limit meets an institution’s legitimate future costs; they do, however, provide no support for the contention that the regulatory framework is shown on this record to render these institutions commercially unviable. Considered with their participation in the process and the provision for conditional enhancement on the basis of audited accounts, the restriction has not been shown to impose a burden plainly excessive in relation to the protection of students and the maintenance of educational standards. The Petitioners’ proportionality objection, therefore, does not displace the conclusion that the Impugned Notifications falls within the reasonable limits of Article 18 of the Constitution.41

Last but not the least, the reliance placed upon Article 25 of the Constitution by the Petitioner Institutions while attempting to compare themselves with institutions imparting other professional education, is unsustainable as that comparison alone does not establish unconstitutional discrimination. Medical and dental institutions fall within a distinct legislative and regulatory scheme, involving prescribed clinical training, institutional recognition and professional qualifications. Differential 41 see pp.244–247, 303–304 | Proportionality in Action: Comparative and Empirical Perspectives on the Judicial Practice | (2020) | Edited by Mordechai Kremnitzer, Talya Steiner & Andrej Lang | Published by Cambridge University Press. Page 27 regulation of that field has a rational relationship with the subject of the PM&DC Act. Equally, common regulation within the field cannot excuse arbitrary treatment of materially different financial circumstances. The equality objection thus does not negate the Council’s jurisdiction, although a demonstrated discriminatory exercise remains open to judicial review as it is trite that reasonable classification is permissible and Article 25 of the Constitution is only attracted in an apple-to-apple comparison42. It is also well settled that although Article 25 of the Constitution envisages equality amongst citizens, it also allows for differential treatment of the persons who are not similarly placed by virtue of a reasonable classification. However, to justify this difference in treatment, the reasonable classification needs to be ‘based on intelligible differentia’, which has a rational nexus with the object being sought to be achieved43. Likewise, it is vouched by the respectable authority that the persons may be classified in groups and such groups may be treated differently, if there is a reasonable classification44. It must also be borne in mind that medical education is intrinsically connected with the preservation of human life and the competence of those entering the medical profession has a direct bearing upon public health and safety. Institutions imparting such education cannot, therefore, be permitted to assume the character of purely commercial enterprises, divorced from their overriding responsibility towards society.

For the foregoing reasons, the instant Constitutional Petition alongwith the two connected petitions challenging the Impugned Notifications are dismissed. The Constitutional Petitions filed by the Petitioner Students, seeking implementation of the Impugned Notifications are allowed with a direction to the PM&DC and the Institutions concerned to implement the Impugned Notifications in accordance with their terms, to the extent applicable to the respective Petitioner Students.
